title: Hostinger Cloud Startup: the deal price is not the long-term price
description: A source-linked calculation of Hostinger Cloud Startup's published first-term total and renewal rate, with unknowns kept visible.
answer: The published Cloud Startup offer is $7.99 per month on a 48-month prepaid term ($383.52 total), then renews at $25.99 per month; that is a source-number comparison, not a prediction of future pricing.
unique_note: The page puts the upfront total, the renewal rate, and the commitment term in the same answer. The multiplication is derived from the provider's displayed monthly rate and term; no unlisted tax, checkout fee, or future promotion is inferred.

sections.heading: Published numbers
sections.body: $7.99/mo is shown for a 48-month term, and the provider states that plans are paid upfront. The published upfront total is $383.52. The same Cloud Startup offer shows a renewal rate of $25.99/mo.

sections.heading: What the term changes
sections.body: The $7.99 figure is a monthly equivalent of the prepaid first term, not a month-to-month invoice. The renewal figure applies after the initial term according to the page. A buyer should compare both numbers before treating the discount as a long-term budget.

sections.heading: What is still unknown
sections.body: The checked pages do not give a tax-inclusive checkout total for this observation, a guaranteed future renewal total, or a precise end date for the rotating offer. Those values are deliberately not estimated here.

title: How to check whether a cloud hosting deal is still active
description: Two tests decide whether an advertised hosting deal is live, applied to Hostinger's own Black Friday and coupon pages as read on 22 September 2026.
answer: A deal is active only if the provider's own page states a date window that contains today and shows the number you are comparing without a checkout step. Read on 22 September 2026, Hostinger's sale pages failed the first test: one page states a window starting 19 October 2026 (27 days later) and another states a window that ended 8 December 2025 (288 days earlier). Neither window contained the reading date, so neither page demonstrated a deal that could be bought that day.
unique_note: This guide keeps two things apart. First, what the provider's pages actually state, each statement tied to the URL it came from. Second, the comparison and arithmetic this site ran on top of those statements, labelled as derived. The day counts and per-month figures come only from the dates and prices printed on the provider's own pages at capture time. No price, discount, expiry, tax or checkout total has been estimated, converted or inferred.

sections.heading: The two tests that decide whether a deal is live
sections.body: Test one is a date test. The provider's page has to state a start date and an end date, and today has to fall between them. A page that says an offer is time-limited without naming the dates has not passed this test, because there is nothing to check against.\n\nTest two is a visibility test. The two numbers that matter are the discounted rate for the introductory term and the rate that applies once that term ends. Both should be readable on the page itself, before you begin a checkout. A page can pass one test and fail the other, and a page that fails the date test is not selling anything today however prominently the discount is shown.

sections.heading: What the provider's pages state
sections.body:
These are statements read from the provider's own pages on 22 September 2026 (UTC). Each one is attached to the URL it came from, listed again under Sources checked.

Black Friday landing page (hostinger.com/black-friday). Its FAQ states that the Black Friday sale runs from 19 October to 14 December 2026. The same page carries no prices at all: it tells readers that savings vary by plan, billing term and location, and sends them to the pricing page for the figure that applies in their market.
Black Friday web hosting deals page (hostinger.com/black-friday-web-hosting-deals). Its FAQ states that the Black Friday web hosting deals were available from 13 October to 8 December 2025, and that the Cyber Monday deals ran from 8 to 15 December 2025. Elsewhere the page says the offers are only around for a limited time without naming a date next to that sentence.
Coupon page (hostinger.com/coupons). The page's own heading carries a month and year. Its FAQ says the size of the saving depends on the discounts and sales available at the time of reading, and that the current deals change on a regular basis. It instructs readers to claim a code by choosing a plan and going to the checkout page.
Pricing page (hostinger.com/pricing). Prices are presented under a 48-month term selector. No date appears on the page.

On the renewal question, the Black Friday landing page states that the renewal price depends on the plan and the term and is shown before checkout. The web hosting deals page states that the full amount due is visible during registration.

sections.heading: The comparison this site ran on top of those statements (derived)
sections.body:
Everything in this section is this site's own reading of the statements above, not a claim made by the provider. Day counts are measured from the 22 September 2026 capture date.

Black Friday landing page: stated window 19 October to 14 December 2026; the window had not opened, starting 27 days after the capture date; no price printed on the page; renewal rate not printed on the page.
Black Friday web hosting deals page: stated window 13 October to 8 December 2025; the window had closed 288 days before the capture date; promotional monthly rates printed on the page; renewal rates printed on the page.
Coupon page: no start or end date, only a month and year in the heading, so there is no window to test; promotional rates printed with an on-page coupon applied; renewal rates printed.
Pricing page: no date at all, only a 48-month term selector; promotional and renewal rates both printed.

The finding that matters is the disagreement. Two pages on the same provider's site, read within minutes of each other, state two different Black Friday windows: one in 2026, one in 2025. Neither window contained the date of reading. So the provider's own sale pages did not agree on when the sale was, and neither described a window that was open on the day it was read.

The same comparison also shows that the promo rate is not a single number. The pricing page and the deals page print the same three monthly rates, while the coupon page prints a lower rate for each of the same plans, with an on-page coupon shown as applied. Which figure a buyer sees therefore depends on which of the provider's pages they landed on.

sections.heading: The renewal rate sits below the stated regular price (derived)
sections.body:
This is arithmetic on the provider's own printed numbers, offered as an observation rather than a prediction.

For the Premium plan, the page states a regular price of $575.52 across a 48-month term, which is $11.99 per month, and separately states a renewal rate of $10.99 per month. The same $1.00 gap repeats on the other two plans: $18.99 against $16.99 for Unlimited, and $27.99 against $25.99 for Cloud Startup.

The pages do not state which term the renewal rate assumes. This is not evidence that renewal will be cheaper than the introductory rate, and it is not a forecast. It is only an observation that two figures published on the same page do not line up, which means the label regular price cannot be used as a reliable stand-in for what the bill becomes after the first term.

sections.heading: What this check cannot tell you
sections.body:
The unknowns are worth naming, because they are the part a deal page tends to leave out.

No page checked carried a machine-readable published or modified date, so the age of the text cannot be verified from metadata. The only date evidence on these pages is prose inside FAQ blocks.
None of the pages stated a tax-inclusive total, a guaranteed future renewal total, or a per-region price. Savings are stated to vary by plan, term and location, so a price read from one region is not evidence of the price in another.
A number printed on the page is not the same as a number guaranteed at checkout. The pages themselves place the renewal figure and the full amount due at the checkout or registration step, which is after the point where most buyers have already decided.
Finally, this check says nothing about whether the discount is genuinely the lowest price the provider has offered. That would need a price history, and none of these pages publishes one.

sections.heading: A method you can repeat in about a minute
sections.body:
First, write down the exact URL and the time you opened it, in UTC. A deal claim without a timestamp cannot be checked later, and rotating offers are the whole reason the timestamp matters.

Second, search the page for an explicit start and end date. If there is none, mark the deal unverified and stop there.

Third, if a window exists, test today against it. A window that starts later, or ended earlier, is not a live deal, however it is presented.

Fourth, sort the numbers by where they appear. Note the promotional rate, then note the renewal rate separately, and write down which of them required a checkout step to see.

Fifth, re-read the same URL a few days later and compare. If the stated window moves, the date is being used to gate the offer. If it never moves while the page still calls the offer time-limited, the window is not gating anything, and the discount should be judged on the price alone.

title: Free migration: what you must hand over, and the downtime it does not rule out
description: Hostinger's own migration and cloud pages, read on 23 September 2026, name three prerequisites, exclude closed-code site builders, and give two completion times 60x apart. Neither page promises zero downtime, and neither publishes a remedy.
answer: A free migration is not a standalone freebie: it is a service unlocked by buying a hosting plan first, and Hostinger's own pages name exactly three things the customer must supply before the move can start - a working link to the current provider's admin area, the account username and password (an administrator account in the case of WordPress), and enough free disk space at the old host to support the move. Sites built on closed-code website builders such as Wix, Squarespace and Shopify are stated as not migratable at all, and a domain move requires that you own the domain and that it has been active for 60 days or more. On downtime, nothing checked promises zero: the migration page's headline offers migration "without hassle or downtime", yet that same page's FAQ says you "might experience some downtime after the migration during the DNS propagation period", and the cloud page only offers to "minimize downtime". No page checked states a downtime limit, a completion guarantee, or any remedy if the move goes wrong - so the free migration is best treated as a convenience with an unpriced risk, not a guaranteed risk-free move.
unique_note: This page separates two things throughout. First, what Hostinger's own pages state, each statement tied to the URL it came from and quoted only in short fragments. Second, the comparison and arithmetic this site ran on top of those statements, labelled (derived). The 60x timing gap and the day-count reasoning come only from figures the provider prints on its own pages. No price, discount, migration fee, downtime duration, credit amount, success rate or customer count has been estimated, converted or inferred, and the cost of the overlap period is left as a formula because the previous provider's rate is not published by Hostinger.

sections.heading: What you must provide before the move can start
sections.body:
Hostinger's migration page answers this question in its own FAQ, and the list is short. It names three items, quoted here as published:

One, "a working link to your current provider's admin area, such as a login screen or a wp-admin link."
Two, "your login details - the username and password. For WordPress websites, make sure the username is an admin user."
Three, "enough disk space at your previous hosting provider to support the migration", with the page adding that you can find this in your control panel.

The same FAQ adds that the provider's "dedicated migration team can also migrate a multisite WordPress website", and it offers a manual route as an alternative, in which the customer downloads the website files and the database and uploads both, with the warning that if you upload only one of the two, "your website won't work."

What the list does not contain is as informative as what it does. There is no published maximum site size, no minimum plan tier named as a condition of the free service, no named list of source control panels, and no statement of who performs the DNS change. The free service is therefore documented as a credential handover with an unspecified upper bound.

sections.heading: What is excluded: the sites and domains that do not qualify
sections.body:
Two exclusions are stated outright.

The first is platform-based. The migration FAQ states that if you build websites using any website builder, you will not be able to migrate them, because those are "closed-code platforms", and it names Wix, Squarespace and Shopify among the examples. The provider's own suggested alternative is to start again with its AI website builder and copy the content across - which is a rebuild, not a migration.

The second is domain-based. On moving a domain, the page states that the guide applies "if you have full ownership of your domain and it has been active for 60 days or more." A domain registered more recently than that does not meet the stated condition, and no workaround is published.

There is also a per-site condition rather than a cap: the number of sites is unlimited with the plan, but "for multiple migrations, you'll have to make a separate request for each website." Unlimited capacity, one request at a time.

sections.heading: Two published completion times, 60x apart (derived)
sections.body:
This section is this site's comparison of two statements the provider publishes on two of its own pages. Both pages describe the same free migration service.

The cloud hosting page, in its feature list, states: "Send a request and we move as many sites as you need, usually in about 20 minutes. Your site stays online while we switch."

The migration page, in its FAQ, states that "a simple, automatic WordPress website migration is typically done in less than two hours", and that "it usually takes more than 20 hours for cPanel-based websites that are built with other open-source CMS."

The arithmetic is simple and worth stating plainly: 20 hours is 1,200 minutes, and 1,200 divided by 20 is 60. So the shortest figure one page publishes is 60 times smaller than the longest figure the other page publishes, for the same service on the same provider's site, read within minutes of each other.

The honest qualification is that these two figures may describe different scenarios - a small automatic WordPress move against a larger cPanel move on a different CMS - and the provider is not necessarily contradicting itself. But neither page states the scope that would reconcile them. The cloud page's 20-minute figure carries no platform or size condition at all, and the migration page's figures are not cross-referenced from the cloud page. A buyer who reads only the cloud page forms an expectation that the other page's own FAQ puts two orders of magnitude away, and nothing on either page tells them which estimate applies to their site.

sections.heading: The no-downtime claim at the top is softened at the bottom (derived)
sections.body:
The migration page makes a strong claim in its headline and a weaker one in its FAQ. The comparison below is this site's reading, not a quotation of intent.

Stated at the top of the migration page: migration is automated "without hassle or downtime", and the provider will migrate your site "quickly and securely, keeping it up and running throughout." Stated in the same page's FAQ: the website "will work smoothly during the migration process", and "however, you might experience some downtime after the migration during the DNS propagation period."

The cloud page shows the same pattern. Its feature list says "your site stays online while we switch." Its FAQ says the site "will still be online during the migration process", and that the provider will "help you prepare for DNS propagation to minimize downtime."

Two things follow from putting those sentences side by side. First, both pages concede that downtime is possible after the switch, in the DNS propagation window, and the word used on the cloud page is "minimize" - which by definition does not mean eliminate. Second, and more usefully for a buyer, no page checked puts a number on it: there is no published downtime duration, no ceiling expressed in minutes or hours, and no stated condition under which downtime counts as a failure. The migration service itself also carries no published availability figure. The 99.9% uptime statement on the cloud page describes the hosting service, not the migration, and the two should not be read as the same promise.

sections.heading: What the free migration still costs you (derived, deliberately unpriced)
sections.body:
The word free applies to the migration service, not to the purchase it depends on. The migration page states it directly: "All you need to do is purchase a hosting plan, and you can then enjoy unlimited free WordPress and other website migrations to Hostinger." On the same page, the plan the cloud page pairs with its migration claim - Cloud Startup - is listed at $7.99 per month on a 48-month term, renewing at $25.99 per month, with the page noting that all plans are paid upfront and that prices are listed without VAT.

The second cost is the overlap. The migration FAQ advises that you usually do not have to inform your current provider, "however, make sure not to cancel your hosting service before the migration is fully completed." That instruction means two hosting bills run at the same time for the length of the migration. Because the migration page also tells you not to cancel early, the free service carries a real cost whose size is the previous provider's rate multiplied by the migration window.

That window is exactly the quantity the two pages disagree about by a factor of 60, and the previous provider's rate is not published by Hostinger at all. So this page does not print a number for it. It prints the shape of the cost instead: cost of overlap = previous host's rate per day x days until the provider confirms the transfer. The provider states it will email you "as soon as the transfer is successful", which is when the overlap is meant to end. The reason this matters is that the shortest published estimate makes the overlap nearly free, while the longest makes it a bill worth planning for - and the page that publishes the long estimate is the same page that tells you not to cancel.

sections.heading: The gap that matters most: no published remedy
sections.body:
The migration gap is not the prerequisites, which are clear, or the exclusions, which are stated. It is the absence of any remedy tied to the migration itself.

The migration page advertises a 30-day money-back guarantee, and the refund paragraph describes it as a refund window on your payment with the note that "exclusions may apply". That is a purchase refund window, not a migration remedy. Neither page checked states a credit, a compensation, a guaranteed re-run, or any remedy at all for a migration that runs long, fails partway, or leaves the site unreachable during DNS propagation.

Nor is a success rate published. The migration page's market comparison table assigns free migration an "included" value against a claimed market range of $30-$100 per site, inside a headline claim of saving $800-$2,400 or more per year against a stated market cost of $1,067-$2,692 annually. Those are the provider's own estimates: the ranges name no vendors and cite no survey, so they should be read as a marketing claim rather than a measured market price. What they do not do is quantify the risk on the other side of the transaction.

The practical conclusion is that the free migration shifts a credential handover to the provider while leaving the buyer holding the timing risk and the DNS risk, with no published remedy if either goes badly. That is not a reason to avoid it. It is a reason to schedule it, and to keep your own backup.

sections.heading: A checklist to run before you submit the request
sections.body:
Five items, all of them derived from the provider's own stated conditions rather than from anything measured here.

Confirm the platform qualifies. If the site was built in a closed-code builder such as Wix, Squarespace or Shopify, the stated answer is no, and the published fallback is a rebuild.
Confirm you hold the credentials, not just access. The stated requirement is a username and password with administrator rights for WordPress, plus a working link to the admin area. A staff account without admin rights does not match the published requirement.
Check the old host's disk allowance before you ask. The stated prerequisite is enough space at the previous provider, and that is a limit you can read in your own control panel.
Take your own backup first. The manual route published by the provider requires both the files and the database, and warns the site will not work if either is missing. Having both, off the provider's hands, is the only remedy for migration failure that this check found published anywhere.
Plan the overlap in money and in days. Do not cancel the old plan until the provider's confirmation email arrives, and decide in advance which of the two published timelines you are budgeting against - 20 minutes or more than 20 hours.

Finally, verify reachability after the switch rather than assuming it, because the only statement the provider makes about the period after the move is that downtime might occur during DNS propagation.

sections.heading: What this check cannot tell you
sections.body:
The unknowns are worth naming, because they are the part a deal page leaves out.

No page checked carried a machine-readable published or modified date, so the age of the text cannot be verified from metadata. Prices and statements were read on 23 September 2026 (UTC), and rotating offers and plan pricing can change after that.
No downtime duration, ceiling or remedy is published for the migration, so the risk cannot be sized from these pages.
No tax-inclusive checkout total is published for the plans quoted here; the pages state that displayed rates exclude applicable taxes and that prices are listed without VAT, and savings are stated to vary by plan, term and location.
No migration success rate, average handling time distribution, or customer count for migrations is published. The 20-minute and 20-hour figures are the only two completion statements found, and neither is given with a stated scope.
And this check says nothing about whether the free migration is better or worse than a paid one elsewhere. That would require the same prerequisites, timings and remedies from other providers, which is outside the two pages examined here.

title: Cloud hosting deals show 6 of the 29 resource limits the provider publishes
description: Hostinger's cloud and VPS deal cards name 10 of the 36 resource parameters its own linked limits table publishes, and the two cloud pages disagree on one number. Read on 24 September 2026.
answer: The plan card that Hostinger's cloud hosting page delivers in its HTML names six of the resource parameters the same provider publishes for that plan, and the page's own FAQ links to the table that publishes the rest. That table, Parameters and limits for hosting plans, carries 29 parameter rows for Cloud Startup. CPU cores, RAM, disk space, inodes, PHP workers and website count appear on both pages; the other 23 rows - among them bandwidth, I/O, parked domains, database count and size, the 10,240 MB MySQL backup ceiling, every PHP memory and upload ceiling, the four OPCache values and the mailbox count - appear only in the table. The VPS deal cards show four of the seven parameters the table publishes for the KVM plans. Two cells are blank on every page read: a backup size ceiling for VPS, and any numeric support limit for any plan. And where the two cloud pages do overlap, one number disagrees - the deal card says Unlimited websites for Cloud Startup, and the table says 100.
unique_note: This page keeps two things apart. First, what Hostinger's own pages state, each statement tied to the URL it came from and quoted only in short fragments. Second, the counts, ratios and comparisons this site ran on top of those statements, labelled (derived). Every sourced figure was read from a provider page on 24 September 2026 (UTC); every derived figure is arithmetic on those figures and nothing else. No price, discount, transfer figure, resource value, success rate or customer count has been estimated, converted or inferred, and cells the provider does not publish are printed as not published rather than filled in.

sections.heading: What was compared, and when
sections.body:
Three pages were read on 24 September 2026 (UTC): the cloud hosting page at hostinger.com/cloud-hosting, the VPS hosting page at hostinger.com/vps-hosting, and the parameters page that both of them link to from their own FAQ. All three returned HTTP 200, and all three are permitted by the provider's robots.txt, which disallows only its special-offer subpaths, cart, API proxy, tag pages and query-string variants.

The link is worth stating precisely, because it is the provider's own signpost rather than a page this site went looking for. The cloud hosting page's FAQ asks what the CPU, RAM, inode and disk limits of Hostinger plans are, and it answers by sending the reader to that article. The VPS page carries the same question and the same link. So the deal pages themselves say the resource numbers live somewhere else.

One limit on the comparison, stated up front. The cloud hosting page delivers a single plan card in its HTML. That card's resource lines - 4 CPU cores, 4 GB RAM, 100 GB NVMe storage, 2 000 000 inodes - match the Cloud Startup column of the parameters table, so Cloud Startup is the plan compared below. Cards for the other cloud plans are not present in the delivered HTML and are not assessed here.

sections.heading: The resource lines the deal card does show
sections.body:
Cloud Startup's card on the cloud hosting page carries eighteen feature lines. Six of them name a parameter that also has a row in the parameters table. Here they are beside the value the table publishes for the same plan:

4 CPU cores on the card; CPU cores 4 in the table.
4 GB RAM on the card; Memory (RAM) 4 GB in the table.
100 GB NVMe storage on the card; Disk space 100 GB in the table.
2 000 000 inodes (files and directories) on the card; Inodes 2 000 000 in the table.
100 PHP workers on the card; PHP workers 100 in the table.
Unlimited websites on the card; Number of websites 100 in the table.

The card's other twelve lines - 10 Web Apps, Access sharing, a free domain for one year, unlimited SSL, 15 vibe coding credits, unlimited mailboxes per website free for one year, managed hosting for WordPress and WooCommerce and Web Apps, CDN included, a dedicated IP address, priority 24/7 expert support, a 30-day money-back guarantee and AI SEO ready - have no same-named row in the parameters table. They are features rather than measured limits, and this page does not count them as equivalent to one.

sections.heading: The 29 parameters the provider publishes for the same plan
sections.body:
These are the rows the parameters page prints for Cloud Startup, quoted as published. The table gives the same 29 rows for Cloud Professional, Cloud Enterprise and Cloud Enterprise Plus:

Number of websites 100; Node.js websites 10; parked domains 300; CPU cores 4; memory (RAM) 4 GB; disk space 100 GB; inodes 2 000 000; I/O 20 480 KB/s; bandwidth Unlimited; database count 300; database size 6 GB; MySQL max backup size 10240 MB; MySQL max connections (global) 500; MySQL max connections per user 100; MySQL max import size 10240 MB; MySQL max statement time 3600 s; MySQL max query time 1800 s; PHP workers 100; PHP max execution time 480 s; PHP max input time 480 s; PHP memory limit 3072 MB; PHP max POST size 3072 MB; PHP max upload file size 3072 MB; server-based email sending 10 per minute and max 100 per day; OPCache memory 384 MB; OPCache interned strings buffer 32 MB; OPCache max accelerated files 32531; OPCache max file size 512 KB; mailbox count 10 per website.

Two things about this table are worth flagging before the comparison. First, it names four cloud plans, while the cloud hosting page's own FAQ names three - Cloud Startup, Cloud Professional and Cloud Enterprise, at $7.99, $15.99 and $29.99 per month for the 48-month plan. Cloud Enterprise Plus appears in the limits table and nowhere on the deal page.

Second, the table closes with two sentences that bound how far any of it can be relied on. It states that the parameters and limits outlined are fixed, that additional resources require a plan upgrade, and that individual resources cannot be upgraded separately. It then states that hosting parameters are subject to change without notice and directs the reader to the provider dashboard for the most up-to-date information.

sections.heading: What the deal card leaves out (derived)
sections.body:
Six of the 29 published rows are named on the card; 23 are not. The 23 are node.js websites, parked domains, I/O, bandwidth, database count, database size, MySQL max backup size, both MySQL connection ceilings, MySQL max import size, both MySQL time limits, PHP max execution time, PHP max input time, PHP memory limit, PHP max POST size, PHP max upload file size, server-based email sending, the four OPCache values and the mailbox count.

In practical terms the omissions cluster in three places. Transfer is absent: bandwidth is published for the plan and does not appear on the card. Databases are absent as a group - count, size, import ceiling, connection ceilings and the backup ceiling all live only in the table. And the application ceiling is absent except for its worker count: a buyer learns that the plan runs 100 PHP workers but not how much memory each request may use, how large an upload may be, or how long a script may run.

The same table also shows why the resource multiple quoted on the deal page cannot be checked. The cloud hosting page's FAQ states that managed cloud hosting offers 4X more speed and 20X more resources compared to traditional web hosting, and its meta description says up to 20X more resources. The parameters table publishes web hosting plans too - Web Single, Web Premium and Unlimited - so a baseline is available. Against Web Premium, Cloud Startup's published 4 CPU cores, 4 GB RAM, 100 GB disk and 2 000 000 inodes are 4x, 2x, 5x and 5x the web hosting values of 1, 2 GB, 20 GB and 400 000. Against Web Single the widest ratio is 10x, on disk space and inodes. No pairing in the table produces 20x. The provider does not name the baseline it used, so this is not evidence that the claim is wrong - it is evidence that the claim cannot be reproduced from the numbers the provider itself publishes, which is the same problem as the missing rows.

sections.heading: The one number the two pages disagree on (derived)
sections.body: The card says Unlimited websites. The parameters page's first row for Cloud Startup is Number of websites 100, and it prints 100 for all four cloud plans. Both statements come from the same provider, both were readable on 24 September 2026, and the deal page links to the table that contradicts it.\n\nThis page cannot say which one governs a purchase. The table's closing note points readers to the provider dashboard for current information, which makes the table the more conservative source of the two; but the card is the page a buyer actually sees before deciding. What can be said is narrower and still useful: a limit described as unlimited on one page and as 100 on another is not a limit a buyer can plan against until the provider reconciles it, and the reconciliation is not published.

sections.heading: Cloud against VPS: the same provider, two shapes of limit (derived)
sections.body:
The VPS cards do better than the cloud card on one row and worse on three. Each KVM card carries four resource lines, and the parameters table publishes seven rows for the same four plans: vCPU cores, memory, disk space, IPv4 and IPv6 allocation, inodes, I/O and bandwidth. So the cards show four of seven.

What the cards print, as published: KVM 1 has 1 vCPU core, 4 GB RAM, 50 GB NVMe disk space and 4 TB bandwidth. KVM 2 has 2 vCPU cores, 8 GB RAM, 100 GB NVMe and 8 TB bandwidth. KVM 4 has 4 vCPU cores, 16 GB RAM, 200 GB NVMe and 16 TB bandwidth. KVM 8 has 8 vCPU cores, 32 GB RAM, 400 GB NVMe and 32 TB bandwidth. The table's remaining three rows for those plans are IPv4 and IPv6 allocation of 1, inodes unlimited, and I/O of 300 MB/s - all three of which the cards omit.

Bandwidth is the clearest case in the whole comparison. The parameters table publishes bandwidth as Unlimited for all four cloud plans. The cloud deal card does not mention bandwidth at all. The VPS cards do mention it, and there it is metered: 4, 8, 16 and 32 TB. So the deal page whose published allowance is unlimited keeps quiet about it, while the page whose allowance is finite prints the number. That is the reverse of what a buyer scanning for value would expect, and it is only visible if you open the table the deal page links to.

One further difference sits in the table rather than the cards. The cloud table expresses I/O in kilobytes per second, with Cloud Startup at 20 480 KB/s. The VPS table expresses the same parameter in megabytes per second, at 300 MB/s. Neither table states a conversion, and this page does not perform one; the point is that a reader comparing those two columns is comparing two different units, and inodes run the other way - 2 000 000 on the cloud plan against unlimited on the VPS plans.

sections.heading: Backup and support: the cells that are not published
sections.body:
Backup is the clearest blank cell, and it is blank in two different ways.

On cloud, the deal page states 99.9% uptime, daily backups and DDoS protection. The parameters table publishes a ceiling for the same plan - MySQL max backup size 10240 MB - but no cadence. So the cadence is on the page without the ceiling and the ceiling is in the table without the cadence, and no page read carries both. A buyer who wants to know how large a backup can be before the free service stops covering it has to assemble that answer from two pages.

On VPS the ceiling is missing altogether. The VPS deal page states Free weekly VPS backups and snapshots, and explains that the service includes automatic weekly backups plus manual snapshots you can use to revert your server if something goes wrong. The parameters table's KVM block has no backup row at all. So for VPS the cadence is published and the size ceiling is not published anywhere this check could read.

Support has the same shape. Both deal pages advertise priority 24/7 expert support, and the cloud page defines it: available 24/7 via live chat, with a median response time of one minute for requests in English, plus support in 10 other languages. The parameters page publishes no support row for any plan. There is therefore no published numeric support limit for any plan read here - no response ceiling, no escalation time, no remedy - and a median response time is a median, not a ceiling.

sections.heading: What this check cannot tell you
sections.body:
The unknowns are worth naming, because they are the part a deal page leaves out.

No page checked carried a machine-readable published or modified date, so the age of the text cannot be verified from metadata. Everything here was read on 24 September 2026 (UTC), and the parameters page states outright that hosting parameters can change without notice.

The parameters table covers cloud plans, web hosting plans, agency plans, VPS plans, game panel plans and several legacy and regional plan families. Only the cloud and KVM blocks were used here; the others sit outside the two deal pages examined.

The Cloud Startup card is the only cloud plan card in the delivered HTML, so this comparison says nothing about what the Cloud Professional or Cloud Enterprise cards show once the page's plan selector is used.

No page publishes a backup ceiling for VPS, a numeric support limit for any plan, or the baseline behind the 20x resource claim. And none of this says whether a plan is good value: a published limit is not a measured one, no resource was tested here, and the comparison is only between what the provider prints and what its own deal page chooses to show.

sections.heading: A repeatable method for reading a deal card's resource claims
sections.body:
Deal cards are summaries, and summaries drop things. The check takes about five minutes per provider.

First, open the deal page and list every line on the plan card that names a quantity: cores, memory, storage, inodes, workers, websites, bandwidth, backups. Those are the numbers the page wants you to buy on, and the list is usually shorter than you expect.

Second, search the same page's FAQ for a question about limits. Providers tend to answer it by linking to a table rather than printing the table, and that link is the signpost that matters.

Third, open that table and count its rows. The gap between the two counts is what the card left out, and it is usually the rows a buyer would care about: transfer, database ceilings, backup ceilings, PHP memory.

Fourth, compare only the rows that appear on both pages, and check the values agree. A card that says unlimited where the table says a number is the highest-value thing you can find, because it changes what you can plan for.

Fifth, write not published in the cells the provider leaves empty instead of filling them from a neighbouring plan. A blank is a fact about the deal, and it is the one thing a deal page will never print.

title: A 99.9% uptime promise pays 5% of one month - and the deal page never says so
description: Hostinger's cloud deal page advertises 99.9% uptime and links to four legal documents. None of them contains the remedy; it sits in a hosting agreement the page does not link to. Read on 25 September 2026.
answer: A 99.9% uptime promise on a cloud hosting deal is backed by a published credit, but the credit is not on the page that advertises the number. Read on 25 September 2026, Hostinger's cloud hosting page puts 99.9% uptime in its page title and in its body copy, and links to four legal documents: its privacy policy, its refund policy, its universal terms of service, and a registrant-data policy. None of the four contains the remedy. The universal terms of service defers it outright, stating that the uptime guarantee "if any, is defined in other documents (e.g., specific Service agreement)". The document that actually pays is the hosting agreement, which the deal page does not link to: its section 7 publishes a credit of 5% of the monthly hosting fee for the month in which the 99.9% figure was missed, claimable within 30 days of the interruption, usable only for further purchases, and subject to eleven listed exclusions. The credit is flat, so a 44-minute shortfall and a month-long outage produce the same 5%. On the Cloud Startup monthly rate the pricing page displays for a 48-month term, 5% is about $0.40; on the renewal rate the same page displays, about $1.30.
unique_note: This page keeps two things apart throughout. First, what the provider's own pages state, each statement tied to the URL it came from and quoted only in short fragments. Second, the arithmetic and the document-trail reasoning this site ran on top of those statements, labelled (derived). The minute allowances, the cash values of the 5% credit and the 3.25x spread between the two published monthly rates are arithmetic on the provider's own printed numbers and nothing else. No uptime measurement was taken, no monitoring was performed, and no price, discount, credit amount, outage duration, claim record or success rate has been estimated, converted or inferred. Cells the provider does not publish are printed as not published rather than filled in from another provider's page.

sections.heading: What the deal page states, and what it links to
sections.body:
Three pages were read on 25 September 2026 (UTC): the cloud hosting page at hostinger.com/cloud-hosting, the VPS hosting page at hostinger.com/vps-hosting, and the pricing page at hostinger.com/pricing. The provider's robots.txt allows all three. It disallows only its special-offer subpaths, cart, API proxy, tag pages, query-string variants and one AI-builder path, and none of those covers the URLs used here.

The cloud page states the uptime figure twice in its own markup. Its page title and its social-preview title both read "Managed cloud hosting | 4X more speed | 99.9% uptime". In the body, under the heading "Stable and secure", it states: "99.9% uptime, daily backups, and DDoS protection so busy days stay online and client data stays put."

The word guarantee appears on that page four times, and every one of them is the same offer: a 30-day money-back guarantee. The word credit appears once, as "15 vibe coding credits (one-time gift)". The exclusions, the claim window, the credit percentage and the document that contains them appear nowhere on the deal page.

What the page does link to is four legal documents: /legal/privacy-policy, /legal/refund-policy, /legal/universal-terms-of-service-agreement and /legal/non-public-registrant-data-request-policy. The hosting agreement is not among them, and a search of the delivered HTML finds no link to it.

The VPS page behaves differently again. It states no uptime percentage at all. Its uses of the word uptime are a testimonial from a named customer, a line about looking after "the speed, uptime, and stability of our physical servers", and a link to a system status page. It carries the same 30-day money-back guarantee, with the instruction "See our refund policy for details."

sections.heading: The chain from the advertised number to the actual remedy
sections.body:
The remedy sits two links away from the page that advertises the number. Here is the chain, quoted from each document in turn.

Step one, the universal terms of service, last revised 15 July 2026. Section 5, "Availability of site and services, beta services", states: "The service uptime guarantee applicable to specific Services, if any, is defined in other documents (e.g., specific Service agreement) that form part of the Agreement." That sentence is the deferral. This is the document the deal page does link to, and it declines to state the remedy.

Step two, the hosting agreement, last revised 28 August 2026. This is the "specific Service agreement" the terms of service points at, and it is not linked from the cloud hosting page. Its section 7 is headed "Service uptime guarantee" and reads: "We offer a Service uptime guarantee of 99.9% (Service Uptime Guarantee) of available time per month. If we fail to maintain this Service Uptime Guarantee in a particular month (as solely determined by us), you may contact us and request a credit of 5% of your monthly hosting fee for that month. The credit may be used only for the purchase of further products and services from us, and is exclusive of any applicable taxes."

Step three, the exclusions and the deadline, which follow in the same section: "The Service Uptime Guarantee does not apply to service interruptions caused by: (1) periodic scheduled maintenance or repairs we may undertake from time to time; (2) interruptions caused by you from custom scripting, coding or the installation of third-party applications; (3) outages that do not affect the appearance of your website but merely affect access to your website such as FTP and email; (4) causes beyond our control or that are not reasonably foreseeable, including, but not limited to, DDOS attacks and IP blacklists; and (5) outages related to the reliability of certain programming environments; (6) interference with internet connectivity at the customer's ISP; (7) interference with internet connectivity that occurs on one of the routes which is the connectivity path from the customer to our server; (8) browser caching or DNS issues; (9) your fault or negligence; (10) interference caused by other parties; (11) violation of our Terms and Conditions. Claims for the failure of the guarantee above can be claimed within a maximum of 30 days after the interruption occurred."

One further exclusion sits in a different part of the same agreement. In the GPU service terms: "The Service Uptime Guarantee set out in the Agreement does not apply to the GPU Service."

So the number a buyer reads on the deal page resolves, two links later, into a 5% credit that the buyer has 30 days to request, measured by the provider alone, and reduced by eleven stated exclusions.

sections.heading: What the published numbers work out to (derived)
sections.body:
Everything in this section is this site's arithmetic on the figures quoted above. None of it is a statement by the provider, and none of it is a measurement.

The allowance. A guarantee of 99.9% of available time per month leaves 0.1% of the month outside the promise. Using ordinary unit conversions - 24 hours to a day, 60 minutes to an hour - that allowance is 43.2 minutes in a 30-day month, 44.64 minutes in a 31-day month, 41.76 minutes in a 29-day February and 40.32 minutes in a 28-day February. The agreement does not define "available time", so whether the provider measures against the calendar month, the billing month or something else is not published.

The credit does not scale with the failure. Section 7 sets the credit at 5% of one month's hosting fee for the month in which the guarantee was missed. It sets no second tier for a longer outage and no multiplier for severity. On the text as written, a 44-minute shortfall and a total outage lasting the whole month produce the same 5%.

The value on the plan the deal page leads with. The pricing page displays Cloud Startup at $7.99 per month for a 48-month term, with a 48-month total of $383.52 and a renewal rate of $25.99 per month. Five percent of $7.99 is $0.3995, or about 40 cents. Five percent of $25.99 is $1.2995, or about $1.30. The renewal-based figure is about 3.25 times the promotional one, because the two published monthly rates differ by that factor.

The ambiguity is the provider's, not this page's. Section 7 says "your monthly hosting fee" without saying which monthly figure it means, and the two candidates above are printed on the same provider's pricing page with a 3.25x spread between them. The cloud page adds a further wrinkle: it states that "the price displayed is the monthly rate excluding applicable taxes" and that "the total price for the plan to be paid upfront at checkout includes the monthly rate multiplied by the number of months in your plan, along with any applicable taxes." The monthly figure is therefore a derived display value for a plan that is paid upfront, not a monthly invoice.

How many failures it takes to matter. At 5% per qualifying month, a customer would need twenty separate months, each with a qualifying failure and each claimed inside its own 30-day window, to accumulate credits equal to one month's fee. Nothing in the agreement aggregates claims, and nothing in it converts a single severe outage into a larger remedy.

sections.heading: The credit is not money (derived from published terms)
sections.body:
Section 7 is explicit that the credit is not cash: it "may be used only for the purchase of further products and services from us, and is exclusive of any applicable taxes." Three other published documents bound what that instrument can do.

The refund policy, last revised 8 September 2026, lists the products available for refund under standard terms and then lists the products not available for refunds. "Hostinger Credits" appears in the second list, alongside items such as paid support services and GPU hosting. So a credit issued under the uptime guarantee is an instrument the provider's own refund policy does not convert back into money.

The universal terms of service describes how credits held in the customer balance behave: they "are non-transferrable and they may only be used in the Account, in which they were acquired", they "will not accrue and Hostinger will not pay any interest for your benefit", they "may expire", and they "will expire after 2 (two) years from their issuance". If the account is terminated, remaining credits "will be forfeited".

One distinction is worth keeping sharp, because the same document uses the word credit in two unrelated ways. The terms of service sentence stating that refunds issued as balance credits are "made at sole Hostinger's discretion and are not mandatory upon the Customer's request" is about refunds, not about the uptime guarantee. The uptime credit has its own wording, in section 7 of the hosting agreement, and that wording is "you may contact us and request a credit of 5%", with the failure "solely determined by us".

The practical result is that the uptime remedy is scoped to future spending with the same provider, expires, cannot be transferred, and cannot be cashed out under the provider's own published rules. The 30-day money-back guarantee the deal page advertises is a separate instrument. The refund policy states that products "may be refunded only if canceled within 30 days of the date of the transaction", lists hosting plans as available for refund under standard terms, and gives VPS hosting plans their own conditions in a separate section. A refund on cancellation and a credit for downtime are two different mechanisms, and only the first one is advertised on the deal page.

sections.heading: Who decides, and where the guarantee stops (derived)
sections.body:
Two phrases in section 7 do most of the work of narrowing the promise. The first is "as solely determined by us": the provider, not an independent measurement, decides whether the guarantee was missed. The second is the 30-day deadline, which starts at the interruption and runs out whether or not the customer noticed it. Neither an uptime report nor a public status page is named in section 7 as the evidence a claim must cite.

The universal terms of service adds a sentence that reads more broadly than the credit. In the same section 5 that defers the guarantee, it states that the site may be inaccessible "for any reason including, but not limited to, maintenance, repairs or upgrades, or factors beyond our reasonable control (including, but not limited to, equipment failure, network issues, other failures or unforeseeable disruptions)", and that "we assume no liability to you or any other party with regard thereto." Read beside section 7, the pattern is a liability disclaimer in the document the deal page links to, and a capped, expiring credit in the document it does not.

The exclusions deserve reading against the headline number, because several of them cover the failures a customer is most likely to meet. Exclusion 3 removes outages that leave the site itself looking fine but block FTP or email. Exclusion 8 removes browser caching and DNS issues, which is the mechanism by which a site most often becomes unreachable for some visitors while staying reachable for others. Exclusion 4 removes DDoS attacks and IP blacklists. Exclusion 10 removes "interference caused by other parties". Exclusion 11 removes anything the provider considers a violation of its terms. What remains inside the promise is a narrower class of interruption than the 99.9% headline suggests on its own.

The GPU carve-out is the cleanest boundary in the agreement, because it is stated as an absolute: the guarantee "does not apply to the GPU Service", which the same section describes as provided on an "as is" and "as available" basis.

sections.heading: What this check cannot tell you
sections.body:
The unknowns are worth naming, because they are the part a deal page leaves out.

No uptime measurement was taken here. This check compared published text. It did not monitor a server, and no page read cites a third-party uptime record. Whether the provider has ever missed 99.9% in a month, and whether any customer has ever received the 5% credit, is not published on any page read.

The three legal documents carry revision stamps - the universal terms of service 15 July 2026, the hosting agreement 28 August 2026, the refund policy 8 September 2026 - but the two deal pages carry none. The uptime claim was read on 25 September 2026 and can change without notice.

No currency conversion and no regional variation was assessed. The prices quoted here are the ones displayed to this reader on 25 September 2026. The pricing page states that "prices are listed without VAT", and the cloud page states that its monthly rate excludes applicable taxes. The 5% credit is stated to be exclusive of applicable taxes as well, so no tax-inclusive value for the credit is published.

And this check says nothing about whether 5% is a good or a poor remedy by the standards of the industry. That would require the same three things - the promise, the remedy and the exclusions - from other providers, which sits outside the two deal pages and three legal documents read here.

sections.heading: A repeatable method for reading an uptime promise
sections.body:
An uptime percentage on a deal page is a headline, and the terms behind it are usually one or two clicks away. The check takes about ten minutes per provider.

First, note where the number appears. A figure that has reached the page title and the social preview card is a marketing headline, and it will be stated there without qualification.

Second, list every legal document the page links to, then search each one for the percentage. If the number is not in any of them, the remedy is in a document the page did not link to, and that absence is the finding.

Third, look for the words the promise is actually made of: credit, compensation, service level, remedy, claim. A page can say uptime many times and remedy zero times.

Fourth, read the exclusions before the percentage. Count them, and check whether the common causes of an unreachable site - DNS, caching, upstream network, third-party interference - are on the list. An exclusion list is where a headline guarantee becomes a narrow one.

Fifth, convert the remedy into what it is worth and what it can buy. A percentage of a monthly fee is not a cash refund, so check the refund policy for whether that credit is refundable, and check the terms for whether it expires. Then write not published in the cells the provider leaves empty - the measurement method, the claim evidence, the past claim record - instead of filling them from a neighbouring provider's page.

Hostinger universal terms of service agreement

title: The same 7.99 in three currencies: what a hosting deal price leaves unsaid
description: Hostinger's pricing pages read on 26 September 2026 show its top cloud plan at 7.99 per month in USD, GBP and EUR at once, with the same 383.52 total, while the regular price, the renewal rate and the discount badge differ by locale. India and Brazil print different numbers entirely.
answer: Read on 26 September 2026, the provider's top cloud plan is advertised at 7.99 per month on a 48-month term in three different currencies: $7.99 on the US pricing page, £7.99 on the UK page, and 7,99 € on the German, Spanish and French pages - with the same 383.52 numeral printed as the 48-month total in each of them. What changes by locale is not the promotional figure but everything around it: the regular price ($27.99, £22.99, 25,99 €), the renewal rate ($25.99, £20.99, 23,99 €) and therefore the discount badge (71%, 65%, 69%). India is the exception, with genuinely different numbers (₹599 per month and ₹28,752 for 48 months). Every figure on all seven pricing pages read is stated to exclude tax, under four different tax names, and the deal page states that the total is only assembled at checkout. No page checked says the price depends on the reader's region.
unique_note: This page keeps two things apart throughout. First, what the provider's own pages state, each statement tied to the URL it came from and quoted only in short fragments. Second, the counts, ratios and comparisons this site ran on top of those statements, labelled (derived). The ten pages were read on 26 September 2026 (UTC) and every sourced figure below was printed on one of them. No currency conversion has been performed anywhere on this page: where two locales show the same numerals under different currency symbols, that is reported as an observation about the pages and not as a claim that the underlying amounts are equal. No price, discount, tax rate, traffic, ranking, click or performance figure has been estimated or inferred, and cells the provider does not publish are printed as not published rather than filled in.

sections.heading: What was read, and when
sections.body:
Ten pages were read on 26 September 2026 (UTC), all of them on the provider's own domain. Seven are pricing pages for different locales and three are the cloud deal page for three of those locales.

The seven pricing pages: hostinger.com/pricing (en-US), /uk/pricing (en-GB), /in/pricing (en-IN), /de/Preise (de-DE), /br/precos (pt-BR), /es/precios (es-ES) and /fr/tarifs (fr-FR). The three deal pages: /cloud-hosting, /uk/cloud-hosting and /de/cloud-hosting. All ten returned HTTP 200.

The locale paths are worth naming precisely, because four of them are not the word pricing at all. Requesting /de/pricing, /br/pricing, /es/pricing and /fr/pricing returns a 301 to /de/Preise, /br/precos, /es/precios and /fr/tarifs respectively. Those redirects are the provider's own routing, and the target URLs are the ones read here. One further path was tested and abandoned: /tr/pricing returned HTTP 403, so the Turkish locale was not read and no price is reported for it.

Every URL above is permitted by the provider's robots.txt, which disallows only its special-offer subpaths, cart, API proxy, tag pages, one AI-builder path per locale and query-string variants. Its crawler policy also carries an explicit block naming AI crawlers as welcome for indexing and citation, with training declined.

Two limits are stated up front. First, no checkout was performed on any locale, so every figure below is a figure observed on a public page before any purchase step. Second, this gap's original source plan listed a PCMag regional-edition URL; www.pcmag.com is blocked from this machine by a Cloudflare human-verification challenge that also covers its robots.txt, so that URL was dropped and never fetched, and the provider's own locale pages were used instead. That change is recorded in the gap entry.

sections.heading: The seven pricing pages, side by side
sections.body:
These are the figures the provider prints for its top cloud plan on each locale's pricing page, quoted as published. The plan is named Cloud Startup in every locale.

/pricing, en-US: $27.99, then $7.99/mo; 48 months for $383.52; regular price $1,343.52; renews at $25.99/mo; badge 71% off.
/uk/pricing, en-GB: £22.99, then £7.99/mo; 48 months for £383.52; regular price £1,103.52; renews at £20.99/mo; badge 65% off.
/in/pricing, en-IN: ₹1,699, then ₹599/mo; 48 months for ₹28,752; regular price ₹81,552; renews at ₹1,599/mo; badge 65% off.
/de/Preise, de-DE: 25,99 €, then 7,99 €/Mon.; 48 Monate für 383,52 €; regulärer Preis 1.247,52 €; Verlängerungspreis 23,99 €/Mon.; badge 69 % Rabatt.
/es/precios, es-ES: 25,99 €, then 7,99 €/mes; 48 meses por 383,52 €; valorado en 1.247,52 €; se renueva por 23,99 €/mes; badge -69%.
/fr/tarifs, fr-FR: 25,99 €, then 7,99 €/mois; 48 mois pour 383,52 €; prix d'origine 1 247,52 €; renouvellement 23,99 €/mois; badge 69 % de réduction.
/br/precos, pt-BR: R$139,99, then R$39,99/mês; 48 meses por R$1.919,52; preço normal R$6.719,52; renovação R$129,99/mês; badge 71% de desconto.

The locale is stated by the page's own markup rather than by the URL alone: the html lang attribute is en-US, en-GB, en-IN, de-DE, pt-BR, es-ES and fr-FR in that order, and the currency symbol that actually appears in the price strings matches the locale each time - $, £, ₹, €, R$, €, €. No page carries a meta geo.region tag or a machine-readable currency code, so the locale is inferred from the language attribute and the symbol, not from a declared currency field.

sections.heading: What is identical across locales, and what is not (derived)
sections.body:
Everything in this section is this site's comparison of the printed figures above, not a statement by the provider.

The promotional monthly rate and the 48-month total are the same numerals in three locales under three different currency symbols: 7.99 and 383.52 appear as $7.99 and $383.52 on the US page, £7.99 and £383.52 on the UK page, and 7,99 € and 383,52 € on the German, Spanish and French pages. That is five pricing pages and three currencies sharing one pair of numbers.

Everything else around that pair differs. The regular price is 27.99 on the US page, 22.99 on the UK page and 25,99 on each of the three euro pages - three different numerals under three different symbols. The renewal rate follows the same pattern: 25.99, 20.99 and 23,99. So within the group of pages that share the identical promotional numeral, no two agree on the regular price or on the renewal rate.

India and Brazil do not share the promotional numeral at all. Their promotional rates are ₹599 and R$39,99, which are different numbers rather than the same number relabelled.

One internal consistency check passed everywhere. On all seven pages, the printed 48-month total equals the printed monthly rate multiplied by 48, and the printed regular total equals the printed regular monthly rate multiplied by 48. Seven of seven, in every currency, including the locale that groups thousands with a period and uses a comma as the decimal separator. The deal page states that same formula in prose, as quoted further down.

What this section does not do is convert anything. A reader looking at $7.99 and £7.99 and 7,99 € cannot conclude from these pages whether the three amounts are equal in value, because no page publishes an exchange rate and this page applies none. The observation is narrower and still useful: the digits are identical while the currency label changes, so the number on the page is not portable between locales without the symbol that came with it.

sections.heading: The discount badge follows the regular price, not the promotional rate (derived)
sections.body:
The badge is the loudest number on each card, and on all five locales where the promotional numeral is identical it is a different percentage. That is checkable arithmetic, so here it is.

Taking the badge as one minus the promotional rate divided by the regular rate: US, 1 - 7.99/27.99 = 71.45%, printed as 71% off. UK, 1 - 7.99/22.99 = 65.25%, printed as 65% off. Germany, Spain and France, 1 - 7.99/25.99 = 69.26%, printed as 69% Rabatt, -69% and 69 % de réduction. India, 1 - 599/1699 = 64.74%, printed as 65% off. Brazil, 1 - 39.99/139.99 = 71.43%, printed as 71% de desconto. All five badges reconcile to the printed regular price, to the nearest whole percent, with no remainder that needs explaining.

Two consequences follow. The first is that the badge measures the regular price, not the deal. Because the promotional rate is the same 7.99 in USD, GBP and EUR, the entire difference between 71% off, 65% off and 69% off is produced by the difference in the regular price those pages state. A reader comparing badges across locales is comparing regular prices.

The second is that the largest badge belongs to the locale with the highest stated regular price. The US page prints the largest regular price of the three hard-currency locales, $27.99, and it also prints the largest badge, 71%. The UK page prints the smallest regular price, £22.99, and the smallest badge, 65%. The promotional figure the buyer is asked to pay is 7.99 in all three. So a shopper who screenshots the US page's 71% badge and compares it with the UK page's 65% badge is comparing two different regular prices while looking at the same promotional rate, which is the opposite of what a discount badge is normally read to mean.

sections.heading: The renewal multiple is locale-dependent (derived)
sections.body:
Dividing the printed renewal rate by the printed promotional rate gives a single number per locale, and that number is the size of the step up a customer meets when the first term ends.

US: 25.99 / 7.99 = 3.25x. UK: 20.99 / 7.99 = 2.63x. Germany, Spain and France: 23.99 / 7.99 = 3.00x. India: 1599 / 599 = 2.67x. Brazil: 129.99 / 39.99 = 3.25x.

The plan has the same name and, in the three hard-currency locales, the same promotional numeral. The renewal step does not. It runs from 2.63x on the UK page to 3.25x on the US page, a spread of about 24 percent of the UK figure, produced entirely by the regular and renewal rates the provider prints for each locale. The UK page has both the smallest badge and the smallest renewal multiple; the US page has the largest of each.

The same caution applies as above: these are ratios of numerals, and no conversion has been applied. What the ratios show is the shape of the commitment per locale, which is the part a single-locale price check cannot show at all.

sections.heading: Tax is named four ways and priced zero ways
sections.body:
Every one of the seven pricing pages states that its prices exclude tax. The wording is localised, and the localisation is uneven in a way that is worth seeing side by side.

en-US pricing page: "Prices are listed without VAT". en-GB pricing page: "Prices are listed without VAT". en-IN pricing page: "Prices are listed without GST" - the same English sentence with the tax name swapped. de-DE: "Preisangaben ohne Mehrwertsteuer", the full German word rather than the usual MwSt abbreviation. es-ES: "Los precios no incluyen IVA". fr-FR: "Les prix n'incluent pas la TVA". pt-BR: "Preços listados sem VAT" - a Portuguese sentence that keeps the English acronym VAT rather than using a Portuguese term.

Four distinct tax names appear across the seven pages: VAT, GST, Mehrwertsteuer and IVA/TVA. The en-US page uses the term VAT, which is the name of a tax that market does not levy, while the en-IN page uses GST, which is the name of the tax that market does levy.

What no page does is put a number on it. Across all seven pricing pages, not one prints a tax rate, a tax-inclusive example, or a worked total including tax. The notice is a disclaimer in the footer rather than a figure. So a buyer comparing the 7.99 headline across locales has a statement that the figure is pre-tax and no way from these pages to compute what the post-tax figure would be in any of them, because the rate is never stated.

sections.heading: Before checkout or after: the deal page answers the question the pricing pages leave open
sections.body:
The gap this article addresses asks whether an observed figure was seen before or after checkout. The provider answers it, on the deal page rather than on the pricing page.

The deal page at hostinger.com/cloud-hosting states, in its own words: "The price displayed is the monthly rate excluding applicable taxes. The total price for the plan to be paid upfront at checkout includes the monthly rate multiplied by the number of months in your plan, along with any applicable taxes." The same sentence appears on /uk/cloud-hosting.

That sentence settles three things at once. The headline figure is a monthly rate and not a total. It excludes tax. And the total the customer actually pays is not printed on the page at all - it is assembled at checkout from the monthly rate, the number of months, and whatever tax applies.

It also confirms the arithmetic in the section above, because the printed 48-month total on each pricing page is exactly the printed monthly rate multiplied by 48, which is the pre-tax half of that formula with no tax added. So the 383.52 printed on the pricing pages is the pre-tax total, and the post-tax total is not published on any page read.

The deal page also hardcodes one figure into prose. Its FAQ answers what cloud hosting costs with: "Cloud Startup - $7.99/month for the 48-month plan", in dollars, on the English deal page, without naming a currency for a reader who may not be in the US market.

One formatting inconsistency sits on the German deal page. Its Cloud Startup card prints the promotional rate as "7,99 € /Mon." with a comma decimal separator and the symbol after the number, and the renewal rate as "€ 23.99/Mon." with a period decimal separator and the symbol before the number. Two number formats, one card, same plan. The German pricing page prints both figures in the first format. This is not a price difference, only a formatting one, and it is reported here because a reader copying the renewal figure off the deal page would copy a string that the pricing page never produces.

sections.heading: The statement no page makes
sections.body:
The most useful absence in this check is a sentence that never appears.

Across all seven pricing pages, a search for the words region, location, country, vary and varies turns up nothing tied to price. The en-US pricing page contains no instance of any of them at all. The word location does appear on the deal page, three times, and every instance is about data-centre geography - "Select a data center location close to your target audience" and the lists of North American, South American, European, South African, Asian and Australian sites. None of the three connects a location to a price.

So none of the pages read states that the price depends on where the reader is. The pages show different regular prices and different renewal rates for the same plan in different locales, and none of them says that this is what is happening, or explains which locale a given visitor will be served.

That is the practical gap this article exists to close. A deal headline of 7.99 is not a complete price until it is read together with three things the page does not put beside it: the currency symbol, whether the figure includes tax, and which locale's version of the page produced it. The first of those is on the page but not in the number; the second is stated as a disclaimer and never as a figure; the third is not stated at all.

sections.heading: What this check cannot tell you
sections.body:
The unknowns are worth naming, because they are the part a deal page leaves out.

No currency conversion was performed and none is published on the pages read. Whether $7.99, £7.99 and 7,99 € represent the same underlying amount cannot be determined from these pages, and this article does not claim that they do.

No checkout was completed, so no tax-inclusive total was observed for any locale. Every figure here is a figure read on a public page before any purchase step. The tax rate that would convert a printed figure into a payable one is not published on any page read.

Geo-detection was not tested. The locale pages were requested directly by URL, so this check shows what each locale page prints, not which page a visitor from any particular country is served by default. The default routing, and whether a visitor can be redirected between locales, is not established here.

No page checked carried a machine-readable published or modified date. The figures are those printed on 26 September 2026 (UTC) and the pages themselves describe their offers as rotating, so the numerals above should be treated as an observation with a timestamp rather than as a standing price list.

The Brazilian page reports no tax notice that this check could find in the same footer position as the others; the Portuguese notice quoted above uses the English acronym VAT. Whether that reflects a different tax treatment or simply an untranslated string is not determinable from the page.

And none of this says whether any locale's price is good value. No resource was tested, no competitor was priced, and the comparison is only between what the provider prints for the same plan in seven locales.

sections.heading: A repeatable method for reading a deal price across locales
sections.body:
A price is a number plus a currency plus a tax treatment plus a locale, and deal pages tend to print only the first. The check takes about fifteen minutes.

First, find the locale paths. Try the language prefix in front of the pricing path you already know, and follow the redirects: several markets use their own word for the page rather than the English one, so the URL you get is often not the URL you guessed.

Second, read the currency symbol that is actually inside the price string, not the symbol in the page header. That is the only place the currency is stated for that figure.

Third, record four figures per plan per locale: the promotional rate, the total for the term, the regular price, and the renewal rate. Then check that the total equals the rate multiplied by the term. If it does not, the page is mixing terms somewhere and the numbers should not be compared.

Fourth, reconcile the discount badge against the regular price before believing it. A badge is usually one minus the promotional rate over the regular rate, so a badge that differs between locales while the promotional rate does not is telling you about the regular price, not about the deal.

Fifth, find the tax sentence and write down what it names and whether it gives a rate. Then look for the sentence that says whether the displayed figure is pre- or post-checkout; on the provider read here it is on the deal page, not on the pricing page.

Finally, write not published in every cell the provider leaves empty - the tax rate, the exchange rate, the statement that price varies by region - instead of filling them from a neighbouring locale. A blank is a fact about the deal, and it is the one thing a deal page will never print.
